html:
After Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium and annexed Egypt in 30 BCE, the grain of the Nile became one of the main food supplies of the city of Rome. Egypt was the emperor's personal province, and senators needed his leave even to visit it.

The yearly Nile flood made Egypt the most reliable grain land of the Mediterranean, as it had been under Ptolemaic Egypt. Taxes paid in wheat were shipped down the river to Alexandria, and each summer a fleet of big grain ships sailed to Italy, first to Puteoli and later to Ostia at the mouth of the Tiber. The grain helped fill the Roman grain dole, the free or cheap bread that kept the city's poor fed and quiet.

Whoever held Egypt could starve Rome, which is why Vespasian seized it first in his bid for the throne in 69 CE. After Constantinople was founded in 330, Egyptian grain was sent there instead, and Rome, now a lesser city of the Roman Empire, relied more on North Africa. The flow ended with the Arab conquest of Egypt in 641.
